## Intuition

Informally, a **game** is a system of interacting decision making agents with
conflicting aims. The flexibility of this definition has led to a wide variety
of games, which can be classified as:

- **cooperative** (players can bind themselves to mutually beneficial
  agreements) or **non-cooperative**;
- **static** (one decision) or **dynamic** (decisions over time);
- **deterministic** or **stochastic** (see [[stochastic-games]]);
- **simultaneous**, **sequential** or **continuous time**;
- **symmetric** or **asymmetric**;
- **perfect** or **imperfect information**;
- **zero-sum** ([[zero-sum-games]]) or **non-zero-sum**.

The mathematical *solution* of a game is an **equilibrium**: a state the game
settles into if left to run (see [[nash-equilibrium]]). The single-agent
problem underlying everything here is studied in [[decision-theory]].

## Normal-form games

Let $j\in\{1,\dots,J\}=:\mathcal{J}$ index the agents, who form the **agent
space** $\mathcal{J}$.

:::{.definition data-title="Strategy space"}

Each agent $j$ selects a **strategy** $s_{j}\in\mathcal{S}_{j}$ (also called
an **action** or **decision**) from the **strategy space** $\mathcal{S}_{j}$.
The joint strategy space is the Cartesian product
$\mathcal{S}:=\mathcal{S}_{1}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{S}_{J}$, whose elements
are **strategy profiles** $s=(s_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{J}}$.

:::

Strategies are typically generated by **decision rules**, functions mapping an
observation to a strategy.

:::{.definition data-title="Pure and mixed strategies"}

A strategy $s_{j}\in\mathcal{S}_{j}$ is **pure** (deterministic). The
**simplex** $\Delta\mathcal{S}_{j}$ is the set of probability distributions
over $\mathcal{S}_{j}$; a **mixed strategy** is an element
$\sigma_{j}\in\Delta\mathcal{S}_{j}$, and $\sigma_{j}(s_{j})$ is the
probability that player $j$ plays $s_{j}$.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Pure vs mixed"}

In poker, a pure strategy for strong hands is "with three-of-a-kind or better
go all in". A mixed strategy is "with three-of-a-kind or better go all in 75%
of the time". The game is random in both cases, but only the second strategy
is itself random.

:::

:::{.definition data-title="Utility function and normal-form game"}

Each agent has a **utility function** (also called **payoff** or **profit**)
$$
U_{j}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R},
$$
giving the utility gain (or loss) for a strategy profile $s\in\mathcal{S}$.
With $\mathcal{U}:=(U_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{J}}$, the game in **normal form** is
the tuple $(\mathcal{J},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{U})$.

:::

With pure strategies each agent $j$ solves
$$
\max_{s_{j}\in\mathcal{S}_{j}}U_{j}(s_{j},s_{-j}),
$$
where $s_{-j}$ denotes the strategies of all players except $j$. With mixed
strategies she maximizes her **expected utility**
$$
\max_{\sigma_{j}\in\Delta\mathcal{S}_{j}}\mathbb{E}_{\sigma}[U_{j}(s_{j},s_{-j})].
$$

:::{.example data-title="Cournot game"}

The canonical model of quantity competition in oligopoly. Each firm chooses a
production quantity $q_{j}\geq0$ at some cost, and the market price depends on
total output through an inverse demand function. It is a static
non-cooperative game with continuous strategy sets whose equilibria are
[[nash-equilibrium|Nash equilibria]] in quantities.

:::

## Extensive-form games

In a **deterministic game tree with complete information** we start from a
directed tree $T$ (see [[graph-theory]]) in which each non-terminal vertex is
owned by a player who makes a **move** there.

:::{.definition data-title="Game tree"}

A game tree consists of a directed tree $T$, a **player assignment** mapping
each non-terminal vertex $v$ to the player controlling it, and a **payoff
vector** (one payoff per player) at each terminal vertex. The out-edges of $v$
are the moves available to its owner, and terminal vertices represent
end-of-game conditions.

:::

Here there are **no chance moves** and every player knows exactly who is moving
and what has been played. Such games are solved by backward induction from the
terminal vertices.

## Solution concepts

The main solution concepts are developed in their own notes:

- [[minimax-and-maximin]]: security levels against worst-case opponents;
- [[nash-equilibrium]]: no profitable unilateral deviation;
- [[pareto-optimal]]: no outcome improves one player without hurting another;
- [[zero-sum-games]]: the strictly competitive case, solved by the minimax
  theorem;
- [[fictitious-play]]: a learning dynamic that can converge to equilibrium.

For large populations of agents, see [[mean-field-games]]; for dynamics driven
by a random state, see [[stochastic-games]].
